messages.subject: Fixing Beta to be the same between two copies in model with two likelihoods
messages.subject_clean: Fixing Beta to be the same between two copies in model with two likelihoods
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I was working on a model with two likelihoods:

rw1rw1joint.formula <- as.formula(Y ~ -1 + beta0 + f(time.ILI, model='rw1', constr = F, hyper=c(0.01, 0.01)) +
                                    f(week.ILI, model='rw1', constr=T, hyper=c(0.01, 0.01)) +
                                    f(time.phylo, w, copy = "time.ILI", fixed=FALSE, param = c(0, 0.001)) +
                                    f(week.phylo, w, copy='week.ILI', fixed=FALSE, param=c(0, 0.001)))

where time.phylo is a copy of time.ILI and week.phylo is a copy of week.ILI. I was wondering if it is possible to specify a constraint in INLA so that the Beta of time.phylo is the same as the Beta of week.phylo.

when using copy, the hyperparameters of 'idx' will also be copied. the
scaling infront of the copy, beta, can be controlled if there are more
copies, using the 'same.as <http://same.as>' argument

f(i, model="iid") +
f(j, copy="i", hyper = list(beta = list(fixed=FALSE))) +
f(k, copy="i", same.as <http://same.as>='j')

meanig that the 'beta' for the 'k' copy, is set to the same (as, point
to the same address) as as the 'beta' for the 'j' copy.

H

messages.subject: WAIC comparisons to other Bayesian engines (e.g., Stan)
messages.subject_clean: WAIC comparisons to other Bayesian engines (e.g., Stan)
messages.body_plain:
I am comparing the fit of a multilevel model fit in both Stan and INLA.  The Stan version has a WAIC value about 10 points lower, despite what seem to be similar specifications.  My operating presumption is that this means that the Stan value is probably a "better" fit and I plan to play with priors / model specifications for the INLA model and see if there are improvements to be made, using the Stan WAIC value as a benchmark of sorts.

But before I get too deep, I just want to confirm that, all other things being equal in terms of model formula and prior specification, that comparing WAIC values between different Bayesian engines is appropriate.  I would think that's the entire point of using a common metric like WAIC, but perhaps it's not that simple.  Thanks.

Jonathan

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] correct Bayesian updating
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] correct Bayesian updating
messages.body_plain:
It is not impossible to deal with the posterior "in its entirety", one way to do it is by posterior samples. Understanding the representation of the posterior made by INLA is nontrivial (a set of integration points and precision matrices).

In other words, formulated in general, my point is:
- If you sample from the prior model, this is (almost) always defined with independent components. So, if you sample the hyperparameter to be 1.7, you sample the beta independently
- If you sample from the posterior, this is completely dependent (since you conditioned on some data), so if you sample the hyperparameter to be 1.7, you must sample the beta conditionally on this value

The reason most models are defined with independent prior components is that it is incredibly convenient. Specifying a prior model where the components have (any kind of) dependency is difficult. And I am no talking about inference now, merely the act of specifying the model, writing it down in a clean way. How would you make an interface for an algorithm that could cover every conceivable prior dependency?

This is why I was saying, in most cases, it might be easier to go back to the "independent prior components defined" model, and fit both the old and new data at once (which is not possible in the case you stated).

Kind regards,
Haakon

If the model does a good job of explaining the data x, then I would expect the residuals to be distributed normally with respect to x.  If residual analysis showed heteroscedascicity, I would infer that my choice of model was not appropriate.  That's a dependence between the hyperparameter and the covariate, though, not beta_j, so ... is there some other kind of dependence you're thinking of?

What is the most simple data generating process and (appropriate) model that demonstrates the kind of problematic dependence that you have in mind, one between the fixed-effect estimates and the hyperparameter estimates? >
> I think that the only way the concern could be specific to Bayesian updating and not model building in general is if there's something important in the model that is missing from the inla result or unsupported as a prior. Thanks, Thierry! POPULATION has four levels and I made them dummy variables using model.matrix. And here is the updated model using iid4d:

nod2.data$VARID.int <- as.numeric(as.factor(nod2.data$VARID))
population <- model.matrix(~0+POPULATION, data=nod2.data)
nod2.data <- cbind(nod2.data, population)
n.loc <- max(nod2.data$VARID.int)
nod2.data$VARID2.int <- nod2.data$VARID.int + n.loc
nod2.data$VARID3.int <- nod2.data$VARID.int + 2 * n.loc
nod2.data$VARID4.int <- nod2.data$VARID.int + 3 * n.loc

inla.res <- inla(BETA ~ 1 + POPULATION + f(VARID.int, POPULATIONaj, model='iid4d', n=n.loc * 4) +
                                          f(VARID2.int, POPULATIONfc, copy='VARID.int') +
                                          f(VARID3.int, POPULATIONfin, copy='VARID.int') +
                                          f(VARID4.int, POPULATIONnfe, copy='VARID.int'),
                 control.compute=list(config = TRUE),
                 data=nod2.data)

The estimates for fixed effect and the variance for the random effects are quite similar between lme4 and INLA, but the INLA estimate for the correlation seems to be more conservative compared with the lme4 as shown in the image attached below. I also compared the same model in brms which uses rstan as backend and same syntax for formula interface to fit multilevel models, which also gives lower estimate. I was wondering why is the likelihood method gives higher correlation estimate compared to the Bayesian methods?

In addition, I was wondering if it is possible to implement LKJ prior for the correlation matrix between random effects in INLA as in Stan?

Mamie

messages.subject: Why is my spatio-temporal A-matrix so large?
messages.subject_clean: Why is my spatio-temporal A-matrix so large?
messages.body_plain:
Dear all INLA-spatio-temporalists

In a toy example I have constructed a mesh with 238 nodes. There are 38 unique locations and 74 data points are grouped over two time periods.

The direct and grouped A-matrices are constructed:

> A.s = inla.spde.make.A(mesh = mesh, loc = loc.st <http://loc.st>, n.spde = mesh$n)
> A.st = inla.spde.make.A(mesh = mesh, loc = loc.st <http://loc.st>, n.spde = mesh$n, group = dat.i$time)
> dim(A.s)
[1]  74 238
> dim(A.st)
[1]   74 2618

Why do I get that many columns of A_st?

I know the answer, can live with it, but does not like it: My group variable is the following:

> dat.i$time [1] 10 11 10 11 10 11 10 11 10 11 10 11 10 11 10 11 10 11 10 11 10 11 10 11 10
[26] 11 10 11 10 11 10 11 10 11 10 11 10 11 10 11 10 11 10 11 10 11 10 11 10 11
[51] 10 11 10 11 10 11 10 11 10 10 11 11 10 11 10 11 10 11 10 11 10 11 10 11

If I correct the timings to start with 1, I get the expected number of columns: 476.

I find this behavior kind of akward. Is it really necessary to rename time periods when you model different sub-periods?
If the answer is YES, what about an error message when anything else than numbers from a sequence starting at 1 turn up?

best
Øyvind

Hi Finn,

Many thanks for your reply. Our model is a spatial model for a point a point pattern and the covariate is distance to a pollution source. So, the linear predictor is a SPDE plus a covariate with the distance to the pollution source and, hence, we want the coefficient to be either negative or zero so that it can assess whether the intensity of the underlying point process decreases with distance to the pollution source. So, actually, we want the coefficient to be negative and not positive.

Another interesting approach would be to model this using splines, imposing an overall decreasing trend on the distance. But I guess that this would be difficult to handle with INLA. So, we'll try with 'clinear' for now, with range (-Inf, 0). Although this case does not seem to be covered according to the manual page of 'clinear'.

Best,

Virgilio

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Why is my spatio-temporal A-matrix so large?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Why is my spatio-temporal A-matrix so large?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
this behaviour is the same for all index-based INLA models (iid, ar1,
etc) so is not related to the fact you have a spatial model.
The A-matrix normally simply reflects what size of model you're
specifying to INLA;
those indices always start at 1.
There could in principle be a configurable warning message from INLA
about this, but definitely not an error message, since that would
disallow prediction to unobserved timepoints and/or locations.

However, inla.stack should automatically compress the columns of A to
only keep columns with non-zero values in them, which in your case
should be the first 238*9 columns.
I think you'll find that inla.stack.A(stack) has a lot fewer columns
than the initial, complete A-matrix.
This doesn't change the INLA model itself, but reduced the internal
size of the eta^* = A eta construction, so is useful anyway.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Isotonic regression
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Isotonic regression
messages.body_plain:
I see. Well, if you're doing an LGCP likelihood, I would recommend
inlabru anyway, since that can construct that automatically.
You'll need to have a look at the latest Workshop slides&practicals
for more information and examples.

We've used clinear to construct monotonic effects, but it's a bit
fiddly; a general spline like model (spde on a 1D mesh) is easier.
For your negative covariate effect, you could use something like this
(see practicals for the spatial covariate technique):

mesh1 <- inla.mesh.1d(seq(cov_mini, cov_maxi, length=knots), degree=2,
boundary="free")
mesh2 <- inla.mesh.2d(...)
spde1 <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh1, ...)
spde2 <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh2, ...)
components <- ~ field(map = coordinates, model=spde2) + effect(map =
fcovariate(x, y), model=spde1) + Intercept
formula <- coordinates ~ field - exp(effect) + Intercept

You want a fixed long range for a spline-like model (and remove the
Intercept or try constr=TRUE in inla.spde2.pcmatern for spde1).
Unfortunately, last time I tried to fix one of the pcmatern paramters
INLA gave an error (have not had time to check where the error was).

Allowing the effect to be exactly zero is difficult, as it rules out
using a simple transformation. In theory, you're allowed to use a
function that actually goes to zero, as opposed to exp(), but I won't
guarantee convergence by the current inlabru iteration method...

For an effect like "distance from something" it would make sense to
pin down the spde1 model at one end instead of an integrate-to-zero
constraint. use
boundary=c("dirichlet", "free") to pin it down at the left endpoint (cov_mini).

Finn

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Isotonic regression
messages.body_plain:
On 9 April 2018 at 12:28, Helpdesk <he...@r-inla.org> wrote:
> isotonic regression is estimation with ordering constraints, like that
> a spline is always increasing (zero included). so that would not work
> in general since it would impose an ordering constraints on some
> Gaussian. you can trick it with clinear, moving that part up to the
> hyperpar,  but only in small cases....

Ah, yes, this is exactly what we used clinear for originally.

Since INLA treats clinear as a hyperparameter, the inlabru
approximation is cheaper (but less accurate).
One would need construct the spline basis more explicitly, with one
effect per monotonic basis function, and do
  basis1*exp(effect1)+basis2*exp(effect2)+...
This is tedious but possible.

There is also a third option: Not imposing the monotonicity
constraint, but hoping that the data imposes it.
If necessary, one can use posterior samples (inla.posterior.sample()
or inlabru::generate() and filter out non-monotonic samples;
this is the same thing as truncating and renormalising a non-constrained prior.
This approach has the added benefit of not presuming too much, and
also to see if the data is informative enough to impose the
constraint.

Finn

Just one more note on using clinear for monotonic spline coefficients:
Since each coefficient will be independent in the prior, this will only give you the highly knot-dependent kind of spline, and not the more wellbehaved continuous penalty splines (that are the modes of spde posteriors).

> effect per monotonic basis function, and do

> constraint, but hoping that the data imposes it.

> this is the same thing as truncating and renormalising a non-constrained prior.

> also to see if the data is informative enough to impose the
> constraint.

messages.subject: Unexpected results fitting AR(1) simulation
messages.subject_clean: Unexpected results fitting AR(1) simulation
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am fitting a number of toy models in order to learn about INLA and latent Gaussian Bayesian modelling.

In this particular case, I have tried to fit a simple time-series. The series is based on a first order auto-regressive latent field with unknown mean, standard deviation and auto-correlation. This example attempts to replicate the first one in section 5.1 in Rue and Martino (2008).

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-Lmpyj-ynzYE/WszoD9SlARI/AAAAAAAAAOM/rmLlgCBHIk0efMkUzKTS1yEVtbaNa3O-QCLcBGAs/s1600/Screen%2BShot%2B2018-04-10%2Bat%2B12.35.58.png>

I use the following code to simulate and fit the time-series:

set.seed(100)
n <- 1e3
nu <- 3; phi0 <- rnorm(1, 0, 1); phi <- .85; tau <- 1
eta <- numeric(n)
eta[1] = rnorm(1, mean = phi0, sd = sqrt(1 / tau))
for (i in 2:n) eta[i] = rnorm(1, mean = phi0 + phi * (eta[i-1] - phi0),
  sd = sqrt(1 / tau))
y <- eta + rt(n, nu)
data <- data.frame(y = y, x = 1:n)
fit <- inla(y ~ -1 + f(x, model = "ar1", hyper = list(theta3 = list(fixed = FALSE))),
  data = data, family = "T")

Obtaining the following results:

> cat("[nu] original: ", nu, " predicted: ", fit$summary.hyperpar[2, "mean"], "\n")

[nu] original:  3  predicted:  5.847902

> cat("[phi0] original: ", phi0, " predicted: ", fit$summary.hyperpar[5, "mean"], "\n")

[phi0] original:  -0.5021924  predicted:  -0.3673144

> cat("[phi] original: ", phi, " predicted: ", fit$summary.hyperpar[4, "mean"], "\n")

[phi] original:  0.85  predicted:  0.8728315

> cat("[tau] original: ", tau, " predicted: ", fit$summary.hyperpar[3, "mean"] / (1 - fit$summary.hyperpar[4, "mean"]^2), "\n")

[tau] original:  1  predicted:  1.498735

Although the results for phi are very close to the true values, all the other parameters are far from the true values. Am I missing something here? Have I mispecified the model? Increasing the number of observations makes INLA crash, so it was not an option for me.

Any help would be deeply appreciated.

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the help. Below, I have addressed some of the suggestions which you made.

1) I didn't consider other aspects of the posterior distribution as I thought that with toy models like this the mean of the posterior distribution would get very close to the true parameter value.

2) AR precision: I was trying to get back to the conditional precision, tau which I believe is the same tau as in the model documentation (https://www.math.ntnu.no/inla/r-inla.org/doc/latent/ar1.pdf), rather than the marginal precision kappa. I am not sure how to go from one to the other with INLA but it is true that it is not a good idea to perform the back-transformation in the way I did. Thanks for pointing this out.

3) I have replace a Normal distribution for the T distribution. The results are much more closer to the true parameters. But my intention was really to understand how to use other likelihood functions.

> set.seed(100)
> n <- 1e3
> phi0 <- rnorm(1, 0, 1); phi <- .85; tau_ar <- 1; tau_like <- 1
> eta <- numeric(n)
> eta[1] = rnorm(1, mean = phi0, sd = sqrt(1 / tau_ar))

> for (i in 2:n) eta[i] = rnorm(1, mean = phi0 + phi * (eta[i-1] - phi0),

  sd = sqrt(1 / tau_ar))
> y <- rnorm(n, mean = eta, sd = sqrt(1 / tau_like))

> data <- data.frame(y = y, x = 1:n)
> fit <- inla(y ~ -1 + f(x, model = "ar1", hyper = list(theta3 = list(fixed = FALSE))),

  data = data, family = "gaussian")

messages.body_plain:
For large n the posterior mean will normally be closer to the true values than for small n.
What is a not-small n? Usually larger than one thinks...

For transforming a single parameter, transform quantiles, such as the median, instead of the mean, since quantiles transform correctly.  If you really need a complicated posterior mean, use inla.hyperpar.sample and inla.posterior.sample.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: Error in fmesher.read(prefix, "manifold") : File 'C:*.manifold' does not exist

messages.body_plain:
I ran into the same issue.  These two things fixed it:

1) Run INLA:::inla.dynload.workaround()
2) Make sure that the values in the triangles matrix range from 1:V, not 0:(V-1).  The latter seems to be common.

Hope this helps.
Amanda

messages.subject: Negative predictions in binomial model where missing observed data
messages.subject_clean: Negative predictions in binomial model where missing observed data
messages.body_plain:
Hi all, I'm running a binomial model on survey data to obtain the probability(Y) among N observations.

My problem:
Some predictions are negative values, which have no meaning as a probability (or as a count, for that matter).

My inla call:
formula <- Y ~ 1 + f(ID, model="bym", graph=idn.adj) +
f(age, model="rw2") + sex +
yrs_educ_agesex +
logldipc_no_oilgas
result <- inla(formula, family="binomial", data=data, Ntrials=N,
quantile=c(0.025,0.5,0.975),
control.family = list(link = "logit"),
control.predictor = list(compute=TRUE),
control.compute=list(dic=TRUE, cpo=TRUE, hyperpar=TRUE, mlik=TRUE))
predictions <- data.frame(NAME=data$ID_1, prov_num=data$prov_num, age=data$age, sex=data$sex,
Y=data$Y, N=data$N,
yrs_educ_agesex=data$yrs_educ_agesex, logldipc_no_oilgas=data$logldipc_no_oilgas,
pred = result$summary.fitted.values[,1], lower = result$summary.fitted.values[,3],

messages.subject_clean: mesh size for continental-scale data?
messages.body_plain:
I'm looking at environmental predictors of nest initiation date in a raptor species that breeds across North America. I have a dataset of >1500 nests in the US and Canada, but the observations are pretty clumpy (much of the data comes from local nest box studies where boxes are placed ~0.5 km from each other).

I created a leaflet map of the nest sites here so you have a better idea of the distribution of nests: http://rpubs.com/jmwiniarski/nestmap2

 Is this distribution (over a huge area, but clumped together tightly in certain places) ok when it comes to creating a mesh? Does anyone have recommendations for building a mesh in this situation? I've attached a copy of my nest locations if that is helpful.

Thanks,

Jay

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] mesh size for continental-scale data?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] mesh size for continental-scale data?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
If I understand correctly you are modelling a quantity that is measured at the nest locations (the initiation time), and not modelling the nest locations themselves.

In this situation, I would recommend one of two approaches:
1) don’t use the nest locations for building the mesh, but just a boundary covering the whole domain, with a uniform triangle size
2) using the nest locations to get adaptive triangle sizes, but with a “cutoff” parameter large enough avoid small clusters.
(In both cases, use a second outer boundary layer with larger triangles to move spde edge effects)

The new INLA::meshbuilder() tool can be used to assess the approximation properties of meshes in a “shiny” way. A separate inla.mesh.assessment() function is also available for command line use. (In the development INLA at least, not sure if it was added before or after the latest testing version)
See the 03_meshes and 03_mesh_assessment practicals linked here for more info:
https://sites.google.com/inlabru.org/inlabru/workshops/26-30-march-2018-st-andrews

Finn

PS. The meshassessment.R file in the same folder as the practical actually contains a version of the assessment code that is now in the INLA package.

See the 03_meshes slides for some more info on mesh assessment. The key is to make the “sd deviation” flat; if triangles are too big compared to the spatial correlation range, the bad linear approximation can be seen by the std.dev <http://std.dev>. inside the triangle being clearly lower than at the vertices. In a “good” mesh, the std.dev <http://std.dev>. is (almost) constant.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Havard,

As per your suggestion, I used a scaled version of dxyz and the results now are consistent across analysis (and in particular say the intercept is consistent with the lme estimate, after getting back to the response scale). I still don't understand why the problem manifests itself as a function of information that the analysis should not use, namely the labels used for a factor defining a random effect. So while I have a solution for the problem at hand, I am missing the overall reason that the problem arose, and hence it's unclear to me what other unforeseen problems might I hit. Are there any situations where the coding of a factor might lead to different results?

This raises additional points potentially relevant for others:

1. Likely my bad, I was unaware of the general requirement that inputs should be scaled. Is that for the response only or also for the independent variables. I can only imagine that many folks do not scale their inputs, in particular the response variable! Does this mean that results from others might have been impacted by this?
2. It would be great if INLA did that scaling internally and then the required back-scaling for reporting results, as the truth is one would like to have all the results on the unscaled scale of the response. Is there a fast way to get results back on the response scale?

Cheers,
Tiago

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for this.

Its for scale/location-scale families of the likelihood, that scaling
of the response can be an issue (any decent scale is fine). For
discrete respones, this is not an issue of course.

Additional to that, covariates should be scaled.

H

messages.body_plain:
I am trying to make a 2d inla mesh that will contain only water. As you can see below, my coastline is open at the edges because water keeps flowing off the edges of the map. Is it ok to use this as my boundary for making a mesh? Or is there some way to "seal off" those open water edges?

#find coastline boundaries by extracting raster cells that border NA values (NA values are land while all other values are water)
RasterBounds <- raster::boundaries(raster, type = "inner", classes = F, directions = 4)
#convert boundary cells to polygon object
pol <- rasterToPolygons(RasterBounds, fun=function(x){x==1})
plot(pol)

#create 2d mesh using polygon as a boundary, with max.edge equal to twice the size of 1 of my raster pixels (1 pixel=100mX100m)
mesh2 = inla.mesh.2d(boundary = pol,
                     max.edge = 200)

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] create mesh using polygon with open water
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] create mesh using polygon with open water
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
If you can extract the coastline as “linetrains”, e.g. as a SpatialLines object, then all you need to “seal off” the domain is to add another set of lines, or a whole polygon, that leads to the combined shape being closed; the mesh will be built on the domain that the input lines&polygons lie “inside” all of them. For lines, that is determined by counterclockwise ordering, I.e. “inside” is to your left as you traverse the lines. I’m not on my laptop at the moment, but IIRC the syntax is
inla.mesh.2d(boundary=list(list(mylines, myenclosingpolygon)), max.edge=..., cutoff=...)
You’ll most likely need cutoff greater than zero to avoid tiny triangles in the fjords.

That said, a mesh of this type will have very strong boundary effects in the fjords.
A more appealing alternative from a modelling perspective is to use the model developed by Haakon Bakka, which has been mentioned on this list previously; there, the mesh stretches over land as well, but with such a short correlation range there that the end result is information is forced to flow in the ocean only, but without the strong boundary effects.

Finn

Hi,

Francesco Serafini and me are creating a tutorial for coastline polygons and meshes, and one for the Barrier model. I put the preliminary versions online because of your question:
https://haakonbakka.bitbucket.io/btopic127.html
https://haakonbakka.bitbucket.io/btopic128.html

When it comes to cutoff, I use 1/5 of the max.edge.length argument. This works out well (almost always). But look at the mesh to see that it does not look weird in places.

Kind regards,
Haakon Bakka

> inla.mesh.2d(boundary=list(list(mylines, myenclosingpolygon)), max.edge=..., cutoff=...)
> You’ll most likely need cutoff greater than zero to avoid tiny triangles in the fjords.
>
> That said, a mesh of this type will have very strong boundary effects in the fjords.
> A more appealing alternative from a modelling perspective is to use the model developed by Haakon Bakka, which has been mentioned on this list previously; there, the mesh stretches over land as well, but with such a short correlation range there that the end result is information is forced to flow in the ocean only, but without the strong boundary effects.

messages.subject_clean: Manipulating predictions while propagating uncertainty correctly
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am running several binomial models on subsets of my data (on Group A, B, C, etc), and obtaining predictions of probabilities of being in each group.  I then need to force all of the predictions to sum to 100%, and I am reporting uncertainty with my final estimates.  When I've used MCMC in the past, I've just drawn 1000 random samples from the posterior distributions of each group's predictions, forced the random samples to sum to 100%, and then recalculated uncertainty intervals from the final posterior distribution created by these combined random samples.  I'm not sure how to do this with INLA.

I've seen the FAQ http://www.r-inla.org/faq#TOC-I-want-to-compare-the-results-from-inla-with-those-obtained-with-MCMC-is-there-any-way-to-do-this-using-inla-
but have not had any success obtaining MCMC results, and I'm not sure this is the best strategy anyway, given the speed and elegance of INLA.

Any suggestions on how to manipulate the posterior distributions of INLA predictions while propagating uncertainty through each step?

Here is my inla call for reference.  Let me know if more details would be helpful.

formula <- deaths ~ 1 + f(ID, model="bym", graph=idn.adj) +
f(age, model="rw2") + sex +
yrs_educ_agesex +
logldipc_no_oilgas
result <- inla(formula, family="binomial", data=data, Ntrials=sample_size,
quantile=c(0.025,0.5,0.975),
control.family = list(link = "logit"),
control.predictor = list(link = 1, compute=TRUE),
control.compute=list(dic=TRUE, cpo=TRUE, waic=TRUE, hyperpar=TRUE, mlik=TRUE))

messages.body_plain:
Sarah:

By “force the random samples to sum to 100%,” are you talking about designating a pivot category among the various outcomes, and then calculating the odds ratios for each other category relative to the pivot in this series of binomial regressions?  If so, and if you then predict over the original full data set and do the algebra to force the probabilities to add up to 1 [essentially, example # 1 under the Wikipedia article “multinomial logistic regression”] then I think the series-of-binomials approach can certainly work and can work with INLA also. The more data you have the better.

In terms of propagating the uncertainties, you can get the uncertainties for predicting each full model by having INLA compute the posterior predictive distribution. This tends to take a long time and gives back some of the speed advantage INLA otherwise offers, but seems like the easiest place to start and you should be able to have some confidence in the intervals that are predicted for each outcome.

However, to combine in the multinomial, you will need to propagate the uncertainty over the various odds ratios just like you are combining / converting the underlying coefficients. Many of the uncertainties in INLA are normally distributed, in which case you can theoretically use the rules for adding / subtracting / multiplying normal errors.  [There is a Wikipedia article on propagation of uncertainty that explains this].  However, I think you will need to do this math step by step for each combination unless you find a good function to automate it or perhaps to propagate the uncertainty by monte carlo estimation. Either way, it is going to involve a fair amount of work.

You could also try the Poisson Trick and convert your multinomial to a Poisson.  There is a FAQ question on this on the INLA home page.  It works best when you have only a few predictors because the required interactions otherwise explode and become unworkable quickly, at least in my opinion. But it is another option and then uncertainty propagation can then be handled largely by INLA through the posterior predictive distribution.

Still another approach would be just to use a Stan package like brms, which offers a categorical distribution that I think would work very well for this, if you have time to let it run with the MCMC. That would allow you to make whatever predictions you wanted without dealing with binomials at all, and you can marginalize the predictions over predictors of your choice, which I don’t think INLA allows you to do.

Good luck.

Jonathan

messages.subject: Cannot recover correct uncertainty with iid2d + Bernoulli link
messages.subject_clean: Cannot recover correct uncertainty with iid2d + Bernoulli link
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
I am starting my first real project in INLA and I have bumped into a weird behavior working with the iid2d latent model with a Bernoulli (binomial) link. Its not a show stopper, but it might signal some deeper problems with my (limited) understanding of INLA. The simplest model where this manifests is:

z_i = x_1 * gamma[t_i,1] + x_2 * gamma[t_i,2]
y_i ~ Bernoulli(exp(z_i) / (1 + exp(z_i))

Where t_i = 1:m is a group index for ith observation, and for each j = 1..m, gamma[j,] is a pair of correlated variables. I am using the iid2d model and the Wishart_2 prior with r = 4, R = [ [0.3, 0.2] [0.2, 0.3] ] (I can a priori expect small effects with substantial correlation, but the problem seems not to be confined to particular parameter values).
Both x_1 and x_2 are binary predictors.
When m = 1, the model behaves OKish, and gamma is estimated well, although some of the hyperparameters are systematically off. But when I increase m, while keeping sample size at N = 50 * m, the estimates are increasingly less calibrated.

To be specific, I roughly follow the methodology from the recent Simulation-Based Calibration paper (https://arxiv.org/abs/1804.06788): I simulate multiple datasets using the prior distribution and then for each parameter I compute the quantile of the simulated marginal posterior where the true value of the parameter is found. Then I plot histograms of those. If the model is well calibrated, those should be roughly flat. As an additional visualisation I plot marginal posterior median versus true value - if the model works well those should be equally distributed above and below the x = y line.

The plots for m = 1 and m = 10 are attached (in between the behavior is more or less interpolated between these two)

The source code to generate those is attached (the actual INLA model is in fit_model function, simulate_data contains the simulation code, rest is helpers for the evaluation).

Is the Bernoulli (binomial) link known to not work well with the iid2d latent field? Or am I simulating the iid2d model wrong (although the same methodology seems to work well with the examples from the manual)? Or is there any other issue you suspect?

Also, I do get an occasional crash which I was not able to pin down exactly, if I find something small and reproducible, will report it.

Thanks for any hints/pointers to literature etc.

Martin Modrák

messages.body_plain:
whenever there is something 'strange' going on, I check with Gaussian
noise with fixed precision. so simulate

y_i ~ dnorm(z_i, sd=1/sqrt(prec))

and set

family="gaussian",
control.family = list(hyper = list(prec=list(initial =
log(prec),fixed=TRUE)))

this is just a check that the coding is correct.

also with logit link, if the random effects are to large in values, you
will often find yourself in the part of the linkfunction with little
information, which makes it even worse.

well, first the 'check that the model do what I want it to do', then,
let me know

H

messages.subject: Spatial RE for 34 locations gets 68 estimates: how to troubleshoot?
messages.subject_clean: Spatial RE for 34 locations gets 68 estimates: how to troubleshoot?
messages.body_plain:
Hi again!  I've been trying to troubleshoot this for a couple days but have run out of ideas . . .

I have 34 locations in my data (variable "ID", numbered 1-34).  In the result, I get estimates for ID numbered 1-68.  Should there be twice as many for some reason (and how would I interpret them)?  Or am I missing something simple about data formatting?

Attached is my graph file and data.  Data are uniquely identified by ID, age, sex.  Below is my bare bones code.

Thanks for your help!
Sarah

rm(list=ls())
library(INLA)

# load the spatial adjacency file
idn.adj <- read.csv("J:/Project/IDN_subnational/data/useful/spatial_adjacent_2_levels.csv")
idn.adj <- as.matrix(idn.adj[1:34,2:35])

data <- read.csv("J:/Project/IDN_subnational/03_cod/sandbox/Group I.csv", header=TRUE)

# Prepare the BYM model and run INLA
formula <- deaths ~ 1 + f(ID, model="bym", graph=idn.adj) +
f(age, model="rw2") + sex +
yrs_educ_agesex +
logldipc_no_oilgas
result <- inla(formula, family="binomial", data=data, Ntrials=sample_size,
quantile=c(0.025,0.5,0.975),
control.family = list(link = "logit"),
control.predictor = list(link = 1, compute=TRUE),
control.compute=list(dic=TRUE, cpo=TRUE, waic=TRUE, hyperpar=TRUE, mlik=TRUE, config=TRUE))

unique(result$summary.random$ID$ID)
# gives 68 ID's  :(

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Spatial RE for 34 locations gets 68 estimates: how to troubleshoot?
messages.body_plain:
On Wed, 2018-04-25 at 11:19 -0700, SarahH wrote:
> Hi again!  I've been trying to troubleshoot this for a couple days
> but have run out of ideas . . .
>
> I have 34 locations in my data (variable "ID", numbered 1-34).  In
> the result, I get estimates for ID numbered 1-68.

Hi there. the reason is that the model=bym, expand into a 2*n vector:
see inla.doc("bym").  the first n component, which is what you're
after, is the sum of the iid term and the spatial term. the last n
components, are the spatial terms.  we need to carry both terms along,
as we need to preserve the Markov property. see

@Article{art585,
  author =       {A. Riebler and S. H. S{\o}rbye and D. Simpson and H.
Rue},
  title =        {An intuitive {B}ayesian spatial model for disease
                  mapping that accounts for scaling},
  journal =      {Statistical Methods in Medical Research},
  keywords =     {year2016,my.own,my.cv <http://my.cv>},
  year =         2016,
  volume =       {25},
  number =       {4},
  pages =        {1145-1165}
}

for example for some details.

ok?

H

--

messages.body_plain:
Hello

I am still struggling with recovering the true theta values for simulated data.
This is very simple SPDE model, in which I am just trying to fit normal linear regression with one covariate and spatial random effect. I generated the GRF values with 'inla.qsample'.

The model results in correct gaussian error terms in the outcome model and correct fixed effect, but the two theta values are completely off from the true simulation values.
I wonder whether this is because I constructed mesh with cartesian-converted values of long/lat.

Below is my code and verbose output.
Any advice or help would be highly appreciated. Thank you!

ps ) I used real data of California census block groups shape files to obtain geographical locations of the centroid of each Block groups.

--------------------
BG.cent.xyz <http://BG.cent.xyz> <- inla.mesh.map(BG.cent@coords, projection="longlat", inverse = TRUE)

mesh.points <- spsample(CA, 2500, "regular")
mesh.points <- inla.mesh.map(mesh.points@coords, projection="longlat", inverse = TRUE)
mesh.points <- mesh.points[order(mesh.points[ ,1], mesh.points[ ,2], mesh.points[ ,3]), ]

auto.mesh <- inla.mesh.create.helper(mesh.points, max.edge = 0.005*c(1, 5), cutoff=0.005)

bg.D <-inla.spde.make.A(auto.mesh, loc=BG.cent.xyz <http://BG.cent.xyz>)

set.seed(1234)
sigma2_y <- 0.5
# fixed effect coefficient
beta <- rnorm(1, mean=2, sd=1) # true value 0.7929
# marginal variance of spatial random effect
sigma2_s <- 1

erange <- 0.3
kappa <- sqrt(8) / erange
theta2 <- log(kappa)
tau2 <- 1/(4*pi*kappa^2*sigma2_s)
tau0 <- sqrt(tau2)
theta1 <- log(sqrt(tau2))

spde <- inla.spde2.matern(auto.mesh,
                          B.tau = cbind(log(tau0), -1, +1), B.kappa = cbind(log(kappa), 0, -1),
                          theta.prior.mean = c(0, 0), theta.prior.prec = c(0.1, 1) )

#spde <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(auto.mesh, prior.range = c(0.1, 0.1), prior.sigma=c(1, 0.5))

Q.true <- inla.spde.precision(spde, c(log(3), 0))

field.true <- as.numeric(inla.qsample(1, Q=Q.true, seed=50L))

proj.BGcent <- inla.mesh.projector(auto.mesh, loc = BG.cent.xyz <http://BG.cent.xyz>)
field.BGcent <- inla.mesh.project(proj.BGcent, field=field.true)

BGperCT <- BGperCT %>% mutate(BGmu=beta*ln_totalpop + field) # we've set alpha=0

# generate Block group level data with BGmu
set.seed(301)
BGsimdata <- rep(NA, nrow(BGperCT))
for(i in 1:nrow(BGperCT)){
  BGsimdata[i] <- rnorm(1, BGperCT$BGmu[i], sqrt(sigma2_y));
}

f.sim.spde <- y ~ -1 + ln_totalpop + f(i, model=spde)

stk.sim.bg <http://stk.sim.bg> <- inla.stack(data=list(y=BGperCT$BGsimdata, nBG_inv=1), A=list(bg.D,1),
                     effects=list(i=1:auto.mesh$n,
                                  data.frame(ln_totalpop=BGperCT$ln_totalpop)
                                               ), tag='dat.bg <http://dat.bg>')

spde.sim <- inla(f.sim.spde,
                      control.comput=list(dic=TRUE), verbose =TRUE,
                      data=inla.stack.data(stk.sim.bg <http://stk.sim.bg>),
                      family="gaussian",
                        control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(stk.sim.bg <http://stk.sim.bg>), compute=TRUE),
                      scale = (nBG_inv)^2,
                 control.inla=list(correct=TRUE, correct.factor=10)

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Could you please supply the summary(spde.sim) output you get?

The Matérn covariance parameters are not consistently identifiable from a single realisation, that’s always a possible explanation.

I’d recommend using inla.mesh.2d instead of the old create.helper function (though they might possibly point to the same code). I don’t see anything wrong with your coordinate transformations, so that shouldn’t be the issue.
However, you can nowadays tell inla.mesh.2d to build the mesh on the sphere without pre-converting the coordinates, as long as you give it a SpatialPoints object with a longlat CRS (or whatever your data CRS is), and specify crs=inla.CRS(“sphere”) as parameter to inla.mesh.2d().
This feature is also supported by the inla.mesh.project functions.

Using random independent locations as mesh seed points is rarely a good idea, so I wouldn’t do that without a specific reason. You can get a quasi-regular spherical mesh with inla.mesh.create(globe=...) for the whole globe if that might be useful. (See the help documentation)

Finn

On 25 Apr 2018, at 19:46, Munji Choi <munji...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hello
>
> I am still struggling with recovering the true theta values for simulated data.
> This is very simple SPDE model, in which I am just trying to fit normal linear regression with one covariate and spatial random effect. I generated the GRF values with 'inla.qsample'.
>
> The model results in correct gaussian error terms in the outcome model and correct fixed effect, but the two theta values are completely off from the true simulation values.
> I wonder whether this is because I constructed mesh with cartesian-converted values of long/lat.
>
> Below is my code and verbose output.
> Any advice or help would be highly appreciated. Thank you!
>

messages.body_snippet:
Hi,

Could you please supply the summary(spde.sim) output you get?

The Matérn covariance parameters are not consistently identifiable from a single realisation, that’s always a possible explanation.

messages.body_plain:
Thank you for the answer.
In my original post, I included summary output under "model results".

I tried using old "create.helper" because I didn't know I just need to specify CRS as sphere - without CRS argument, inla.mesh.2d gave an error.

Now I have another question regarding setting a range value for spde construction.
If I convert into XYZ, the constructed mesh is based on unit radius.
If my guess on the plausible range value on the actual earth scale is 2.2 km (i calculated this value using long/lat coordinates and Haversine distance),
how should I scale this 2.2 km in unit-sphere case?
should I use 2.2 km/ 6378 ?

I'll look forward your comments!

Munji

On Wednesday, April 25, 2018 at 5:40:34 PM UTC-4, Finn Lindgren wrote:

> Hi,
>
> Could you please supply the summary(spde.sim) output you get?
>
> The Matérn covariance parameters are not consistently identifiable from a single realisation, that’s always a possible explanation.
>
> I’d recommend using inla.mesh.2d instead of the old create.helper function (though they might possibly point to the same code). I don’t see anything wrong with your coordinate transformations, so that shouldn’t be the issue.
> However, you can nowadays tell inla.mesh.2d to build the mesh on the sphere without pre-converting the coordinates, as long as you give it a SpatialPoints object with a longlat CRS (or whatever your data CRS is), and specify crs=inla.CRS(“sphere”) as parameter to inla.mesh.2d().
> This feature is also supported by the inla.mesh.project functions.
>
> Using random independent locations as mesh seed points is rarely a good idea, so I wouldn’t do that without a specific reason. You can get a quasi-regular spherical mesh with inla.mesh.create(globe=...) for the whole globe if that might be useful. (See the help documentation)

>
> Finn
>
> On 25 Apr 2018, at 19:46, Munji Choi <munji...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> > Hello
> >
> > I am still struggling with recovering the true theta values for simulated data.
> > This is very simple SPDE model, in which I am just trying to fit normal linear regression with one covariate and spatial random effect. I generated the GRF values with 'inla.qsample'.
> >
> > The model results in correct gaussian error terms in the outcome model and correct fixed effect, but the two theta values are completely off from the true simulation values.
> > I wonder whether this is because I constructed mesh with cartesian-converted values of long/lat.
> >
> > Below is my code and verbose output.
> > Any advice or help would be highly appreciated. Thank you!
> >
> >
> > ps ) I used real data of California census block groups shape files to obtain geographical locations of the centroid of each Block groups.
> >
> > --------------------
> > BG.cent.xyz <http://BG.cent.xyz> <- inla.mesh.map(BG.cent@coords, projection="longlat", inverse = TRUE)
> >
> > mesh.points <- spsample(CA, 2500, "regular")
> > mesh.points <- inla.mesh.map(mesh.points@coords, projection="longlat", inverse = TRUE)
> > mesh.points <- mesh.points[order(mesh.points[ ,1], mesh.points[ ,2], mesh.points[ ,3]), ]
> >
> > auto.mesh <- inla.mesh.create.helper(mesh.points, max.edge = 0.005*c(1, 5), cutoff=0.005)
> >
> > bg.D <-inla.spde.make.A(auto.mesh, loc=BG.cent.xyz <http://BG.cent.xyz>)
> >
> > set.seed(1234)
> > sigma2_y <- 0.5
> > # fixed effect coefficient
> > beta <- rnorm(1, mean=2, sd=1) # true value 0.7929
> > # marginal variance of spatial random effect
> > sigma2_s <- 1
> >
> > erange <- 0.3
> > kappa <- sqrt(8) / erange
> > theta2 <- log(kappa)
> > tau2 <- 1/(4*pi*kappa^2*sigma2_s)
> > tau0 <- sqrt(tau2)
> > theta1 <- log(sqrt(tau2))
> >
> > spde <- inla.spde2.matern(auto.mesh,
> >                           B.tau = cbind(log(tau0), -1, +1), B.kappa = cbind(log(kappa), 0, -1),
> >                           theta.prior.mean = c(0, 0), theta.prior.prec = c(0.1, 1) )
> >
> > #spde <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(auto.mesh, prior.range = c(0.1, 0.1), prior.sigma=c(1, 0.5))
> >
> > Q.true <- inla.spde.precision(spde, c(log(3), 0))
> >
> > field.true <- as.numeric(inla.qsample(1, Q=Q.true, seed=50L))
> >
> > proj.BGcent <- inla.mesh.projector(auto.mesh, loc = BG.cent.xyz <http://BG.cent.xyz>)
> > field.BGcent <- inla.mesh.project(proj.BGcent, field=field.true)
> >
> > BGperCT <- BGperCT %>% mutate(BGmu=beta*ln_totalpop + field) # we've set alpha=0
> >
> > # generate Block group level data with BGmu
> > set.seed(301)
> > BGsimdata <- rep(NA, nrow(BGperCT))
> > for(i in 1:nrow(BGperCT)){
> >   BGsimdata[i] <- rnorm(1, BGperCT$BGmu[i], sqrt(sigma2_y));
> > }
> >
> > f.sim.spde <- y ~ -1 + ln_totalpop + f(i, model=spde)
> >
> > stk.sim.bg <http://stk.sim.bg> <- inla.stack(data=list(y=BGperCT$BGsimdata, nBG_inv=1), A=list(bg.D,1),

messages.body_plain:
Ah, I missed that, sorry.
Those theta results perfectly match your true parameters; theta1=log(3) is just above 1, as is the posterior mean; and 0 is also in the credible interval for theta2.
To see that in the natural scale (range and variance), please use inla.spde.result()

If you use inla.spde2.pcmatern, the summary output will already be on the range&sigma scale, but I nla.spde.result() is consistent between the two models.

Finn

On 25 Apr 2018, at 22:45, Munji Choi <munji...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Thank you for the answer.
> In my original post, I included summary output under "model results".

>

> Munji
>
> On Wednesday, April 25, 2018 at 5:40:34 PM UTC-4, Finn Lindgren wrote:

> > Hi,
> >
> > Could you please supply the summary(spde.sim) output you get?
> >
> > The Matérn covariance parameters are not consistently identifiable from a single realisation, that’s always a possible explanation.
> >
> > I’d recommend using inla.mesh.2d instead of the old create.helper function (though they might possibly point to the same code). I don’t see anything wrong with your coordinate transformations, so that shouldn’t be the issue.
> > However, you can nowadays tell inla.mesh.2d to build the mesh on the sphere without pre-converting the coordinates, as long as you give it a SpatialPoints object with a longlat CRS (or whatever your data CRS is), and specify crs=inla.CRS(“sphere”) as parameter to inla.mesh.2d().
> > This feature is also supported by the inla.mesh.project functions.
> >
> > Using random independent locations as mesh seed points is rarely a good idea, so I wouldn’t do that without a specific reason. You can get a quasi-regular spherical mesh with inla.mesh.create(globe=...) for the whole globe if that might be useful. (See the help documentation)

Ah, I missed that, sorry.
Those theta results perfectly match your true parameters; theta1=log(3) is just above 1, as is the posterior mean; and 0 is also in the credible interval for theta2.
To see t

messages.body_plain:
Yes, that range rescaling is the correct approach. (The code can actually in theory handle spheres of other radii, but I’m not convinced that _all_ of the code would do the right thing, so sticking to the unit radius globe is safer.)

The CRS feature is relatively new!

Finn

On 25 Apr 2018, at 22:51, Munji Choi <munji...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Thank you for the answer.
> In my original post, I included summary output under "model results".
>
> I tried using old "create.helper" because I didn't know I just need to specify CRS as sphere - without CRS argument, inla.mesh.2d gave an error.
>
> Now I have another question regarding setting a range value for spde construction.
> If I convert into XYZ, the constructed mesh is based on unit radius.
> If my guess on the plausible range value on the actual earth scale is 2.2 km (i calculated this value using long/lat coordinates and Haversine distance),
> how should I scale this 2.2 km in unit-sphere case?
> should I use 2.2 km/ 6378 ?
>
>
> I'll look forward your comments!
>
> Munji
>
> On Wednesday, April 25, 2018 at 5:40:34 PM UTC-4, Finn Lindgren wrote:
> > Hi,
> >
> > Could you please supply the summary(spde.sim) output you get?
> >
> > The Matérn covariance parameters are not consistently identifiable from a single realisation, that’s always a possible explanation.
> >
> > I’d recommend using inla.mesh.2d instead of the old create.helper function (though they might possibly point to the same code). I don’t see anything wrong with your coordinate transformations, so that shouldn’t be the issue.
> > However, you can nowadays tell inla.mesh.2d to build the mesh on the sphere without pre-converting the coordinates, as long as you give it a SpatialPoints object with a longlat CRS (or whatever your data CRS is), and specify crs=inla.CRS(“sphere”) as parameter to inla.mesh.2d().
> > This feature is also supported by the inla.mesh.project functions.
> >
> > Using random independent locations as mesh seed points is rarely a good idea, so I wouldn’t do that without a specific reason. You can get a quasi-regular spherical mesh with inla.mesh.create(globe=...) for the whole globe if that might be useful. (See the help documentation)
> >
> > Finn
> >
> > On 25 Apr 2018, at 19:46, Munji Choi <munji...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > > Hello
> > >
> > > I am still struggling with recovering the true theta values for simulated data.
> > > This is very simple SPDE model, in which I am just trying to fit normal linear regression with one covariate and spatial random effect. I generated the GRF values with 'inla.qsample'.
> > >
> > > The model results in correct gaussian error terms in the outcome model and correct fixed effect, but the two theta values are completely off from the true simulation values.
> > > I wonder whether this is because I constructed mesh with cartesian-converted values of long/lat.
> > >
> > > Below is my code and verbose output.
> > > Any advice or help would be highly appreciated. Thank you!
> > >
> > >
> > > ps ) I used real data of California census block groups shape files to obtain geographical locations of the centroid of each Block groups.
> > >
> > > --------------------
> > > BG.cent.xyz <http://BG.cent.xyz> <- inla.mesh.map(BG.cent@coords, projection="longlat", inverse = TRUE)
> > >
> > > mesh.points <- spsample(CA, 2500, "regular")
> > > mesh.points <- inla.mesh.map(mesh.points@coords, projection="longlat", inverse = TRUE)
> > > mesh.points <- mesh.points[order(mesh.points[ ,1], mesh.points[ ,2], mesh.points[ ,3]), ]
> > >
> > > auto.mesh <- inla.mesh.create.helper(mesh.points, max.edge = 0.005*c(1, 5), cutoff=0.005)
> > >
> > > bg.D <-inla.spde.make.A(auto.mesh, loc=BG.cent.xyz <http://BG.cent.xyz>)
> > >
> > > set.seed(1234)
> > > sigma2_y <- 0.5
> > > # fixed effect coefficient
> > > beta <- rnorm(1, mean=2, sd=1) # true value 0.7929
> > > # marginal variance of spatial random effect
> > > sigma2_s <- 1
> > >
> > > erange <- 0.3
> > > kappa <- sqrt(8) / erange
> > > theta2 <- log(kappa)
> > > tau2 <- 1/(4*pi*kappa^2*sigma2_s)
> > > tau0 <- sqrt(tau2)
> > > theta1 <- log(sqrt(tau2))
> > >
> > > spde <- inla.spde2.matern(auto.mesh,
> > >                           B.tau = cbind(log(tau0), -1, +1), B.kappa = cbind(log(kappa), 0, -1),
> > >                           theta.prior.mean = c(0, 0), theta.prior.prec = c(0.1, 1) )
> > >
> > > #spde <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(auto.mesh, prior.range = c(0.1, 0.1), prior.sigma=c(1, 0.5))
> > >
> > > Q.true <- inla.spde.precision(spde, c(log(3), 0))
> > >
> > > field.true <- as.numeric(inla.qsample(1, Q=Q.true, seed=50L))
> > >
> > > proj.BGcent <- inla.mesh.projector(auto.mesh, loc = BG.cent.xyz <http://BG.cent.xyz>)
> > > field.BGcent <- inla.mesh.project(proj.BGcent, field=field.true)
> > >
> > > BGperCT <- BGperCT %>% mutate(BGmu=beta*ln_totalpop + field) # we've set alpha=0
> > >
> > > # generate Block group level data with BGmu
> > > set.seed(301)
> > > BGsimdata <- rep(NA, nrow(BGperCT))
> > > for(i in 1:nrow(BGperCT)){
> > >   BGsimdata[i] <- rnorm(1, BGperCT$BGmu[i], sqrt(sigma2_y));
> > > }
> > >
> > > f.sim.spde <- y ~ -1 + ln_totalpop + f(i, model=spde)
> > >

messages.subject: INLA crash message
messages.subject_clean: INLA crash message
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone -- I was wondering if someone might be able to help me sort through this error message that I received while running the INLA model. I've attached an error text that I received, and will put the code below that I ran. A helpful note is that the "dataforfit" variable we are using is of size 4255, and the "datapred" variable we are using is of size 4255. We've ran the following code in other geographic areas with sometimes larger numbers of houses for dataforfit and datapred, but for some reason are receiving an error with one such model run. Any help would be really appreciated!:

# create datasets of observations
dataforfit <- df[which(df$outcome == 1 | df$outcome == 0),]
datapred <- df[which(df$insptime == 4),]

# print out number of observations of each timestep
print(paste0("Number of observations from time step 1: ", length(which(dataforfit$insptime == 1))))
print(paste0("Number of observations from time step 2: ", length(which(dataforfit$insptime == 2))))
print(paste0("Number of observations from time step 3: ", length(which(dataforfit$insptime == 3))))
print(paste0("Number of observations from time step 4: ", length(which(dataforfit$insptime == 4))))

# print out sizes of dataforfit and datapred
print(paste0("Size of dataforfit: ", nrow(dataforfit)))
print(paste0("Size of datapred: ", nrow(datapred)))

# define time dimension
k <- length(unique(df$insptime))

# define two coordinate matrices
coords1<- cbind(dataforfit$LONGITUDEscale, dataforfit$LATITUDEscale)
coords <- cbind(datapred$LONGITUDEscale, datapred$LATITUDEscale)

# create mesh
mesh1 <- inla.mesh.2d(coords1, max.edge=c(50*S,50*S), cutoff=0.2)

# create two A matrices
A.est <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh=mesh1,
                          loc=coords1,
                          group=dataforfit$insptime,n.group=k)

A.prd <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh=mesh1, loc=coords, group=datapred$insptime)

# create SPDE object of Matern covariance matrix
spde <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh1,
                          alpha=2,
                          theta.prior.mean=c(8,-5),
                          theta.prior.prec=c(50,50))

# create mesh index
mesh.index <- inla.spde.make.index(name='spatial',
                                   n.spde=spde$n.spde,n.group=k)

# create stack object for data for fit
stack.est =
  inla.stack(data=list(y=dataforfit$outcome),
             A=list(A.est,1),
             effects=
               list(c(mesh.index,list(Intercept=1)),
                    list(
                      not_sprayed=dataforfit$not_sprayed)),
             tag="est")

# create stack object for data for prediction
stack.pred =
  inla.stack(data=list(y=datapred$outcome),
             A=list(A.prd,1),
             effects=
               list(c(mesh.index,list(Intercept=1)),
                    list(
                      not_sprayed=datapred$not_sprayed)),
             tag="pred")

# combine stack objects
stack = inla.stack(stack.est, stack.pred)

# formula to input into INLA
formula <- y ~ -1 + Intercept + not_sprayed + f(spatial,
                                                model=spde,
                                                group=spatial.group,
                                                control.group=list(model='ar1',
                                                                   hyper=list(theta=list(prior='pccor1', param=c(0, 0.9)))))

#===================================================================================
# IVc. Run INLA model
#===================================================================================

# priors are set by control.fixed
result <- inla(formula,
               data = inla.stack.data(stack, spde=spde),
               family = c("binomial"),verbose=TRUE,
               #control.predictor = list(A=inla.stack.A(stack), compute=TRUE,link=1)  # Produces estimates
               control.predictor = list(A=inla.stack.A(stack), compute=TRUE,link=1)
               ,control.inla = list(reordering = "metis")
               ,control.fixed = list(mean = list(Intercept=-6.9, not_sprayed=1.97), # Prior means,obtain form Corentin model
                                     prec = list(Intercept=50, not_sprayed=50))  #inverse of the variance
               #,num.threads=4  # uses 4 cores may be helpful
)

messages.body_plain:
Thank you both so much! I think I finally got it to work using a mixture of both of your code, plus guidance from this post: https://gis.stackexchange.com/questions/187798/create-polygons-of-the-extents-of-a-given-raster-in-r

Here is what I did:

#extracted extent from my raster
e <- extent(raster1)
#turned extent into SpatialPolygons object to create the overall 'study space' polygon
p <- as(e, 'SpatialPolygons')
#got a polygon that surrounds cells in raster that are not NA to create the 'water' polygon
#first made a raster containing only the water cells (excluded land cells, which were NAs)
r <- raster1 > -Inf
#then converted water raster to polygons (you need to have package 'rgeos' installed for this to work)
pp <- rasterToPolygons(r, dissolve = T)

#plot study space polygon
plot(p, lwd=5, border='red')

#plot water polygon on top of it
plot(pp, lwd=3, border='blue')
#create mesh, with pp (the water polygon) on the left because it is inside the study space polygon, p
mesh1 <- inla.mesh.2d(boundary=list(list(pp, p)), max.edge=c(1000,2000), cutoff=200)
#plot mesh
plot(mesh1)

I do have a few additional questions: each pixel in my original raster was 100m by 100m and I have covariate data for each pixel that I want to use in an R inla bayesian spatial regression model. Does that mean that there should be a triangle for each pixel? If yes, should I change the max edge to 100?

Also, what determines the amount of land the mesh stretches over in the Haakon Bakka model? Is the short correlation range dictated by the cutoff being 1/5 of the max edge?

Is this mesh only used to help the model decide where to predict the results spatially, or does the extent of the mesh need to match the data points perfectly?

Thank you again!!

For lines, that is determined by counterclockwise ordering, I.e. “inside” is to your left as you traverse the lines. I’m not on my laptop at the moment, but IIRC the syntax is
> > inla.mesh.2d(boundary=list(list(mylines, myenclosingpolygon)), max.edge=..., cutoff=...)
